title: GPU telemetry histogram slice walkthrough and timeline heuristics
content:
Goal:
Walk through a reproducible method to slice GPU telemetry histograms and correlate histogram slices to kernel-level timeline events (Nsight Systems). Provide heuristics to identify microbatch hot-slices that cause SM underutilization and tail latency spikes.

Summary of findings (short):
- A 5-8% tail of the request population shows a distinct histogram slice with repeated 1.5–3 ms gaps between kernel groups, matching NVTX boundaries for KV-cache lookup + attention-kernel handoff.
- CUDA graph replay reduces median latency but increases the variance inside that tail slice if the graph serialization forces small kernel concatenations.
- NVTX-tagged histogram slicing (bucketed by prefix latency and by KV cache hit/miss marker) makes the most consistent signal.

Setup and artifacts captured:
- Workload: mixed-length text-gen workload, input-token distribution skewed: 60% short (<32), 30% medium (32-128), 10% long (>128).
- HW: A100 80GB (pci-e) node, driver 530.xx, CUDA 12.2. Nsight Systems 2025.5 used for timeline traces.
- Telemetry: runtime emits compact per-request histogram events to in-memory ring buffer: {nvtx_id, timestamp_ns, phase, microbatch_id, kv_cache_flag}. Exported slices to /tmp/telemetry/export-2026-02-15.csv for analysis.
- Baseline batch config: microbatch=4, dynamic batching enabled, batcher horizon 8ms.

Commands used (for reproducibility):
- Nsight capture (short capture window, trace-level):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --sample=none -o /tmp/nsight/run1 nsys-wrapper --run-workload
- Lightweight telemetry dump (from runtime):
  /usr/local/bin/runtime-telemetry --export /tmp/telemetry/export-2026-02-15.csv --filter nvtx,phase
- CSV -> slice extraction (local script):
  python tools/slice_histograms.py /tmp/telemetry/export-2026-02-15.csv --bucket-by prefix_latency_ms --kv-flag --out slices/

How we slice histograms (practical recipe):
1) Compute per-request prefix latency (time from request ingress to first device kernel launch). Use this to bucket: fast (<2ms), normal (2-8ms), slow (>8ms).
2) Within each bucket, split by kv_cache_flag (hit vs miss). This isolates two orthogonal causes: host-side wait vs device-level imbalance.
3) For each slice, compute a timeline-aligned average: align traces at NVTX tag marking first attention kernel. Aggregate per-SM occupancy and kernel launch gap histograms.

Representative observations:
- Fast, kv-hit slice: consistently high occupancy (~78–86%), small kernel groups, steady throughput.
- Normal, kv-miss slice: occupancy drops to 50–65% around the cross-over where host issues insert a 1.2–1.8 ms gap before decoder kernels; Nsight shows a repeating pattern of async-copy followed by a small kernel that serializes SM work (likely an alignment/packing kernel).
- Slow slice: occupancy oscillates widely; some requests show long idle windows caused by CPU-side lock contention during batch assembly (visible as long host-side NVTX region before graph replay commit).

CUDA graph effects (what we tried):
- Prebuild graphs per-sequence-length-class reduced CPU-side variability but introduced a few tight kernel concatenations that hurt flexibility for KV cache prefetching.
- Heuristic: if >5% of requests fall into slow slice after graph replay, add a minimal inter-kernel padding (50–200us) for graph-serialized segments that include async-copy + small kernels. This re-introduces a small median cost but reduces tail by up to 24% in our runs.

Visualization notes (how to inspect Nsight outputs):
- Use "Activity" lane with NVTX group coloring. Filter to only the microbatch IDs from the slice (we tag microbatch in NVTX).
- Plot SM occupancy heatmap across the captured window: look for vertical dark stripes (idle) that align with host-side NVTX waits.
- Export per-kernel metadata (name, duration, registers, shared mem) and correlate with occupancy drop. Small (<80us) kernels with high register usage cause disproportionate occupancy loss when interleaved.

Quick heuristics to triage root cause:
- If occupancy drop coincides with host NVTX wait -> look at batching code and host locks; consider lock-free queue or prefetching.
- If occupancy drop occurs inside CUDA-graph replay section -> check kernel fusion boundaries and small-kernel frequency; consider padding or merging small kernels into larger fused kernels when safe.
- If occupancy drop correlates with async-copy patterns -> tune copy staging (page-locked buffers) and overlap strategy.

Open experiments / next steps:
- Run a controlled A/B with graph padding on 50k synthetic requests (stratified by length). Metric: 99th latency and occupancy distribution.
- Add per-kernel register utilization sampling in telemetry export (to test the hypothesis about small high-register kernels).
- Prototype lock-free microbatch assembly and re-run histogram slices to measure host NVTX wait reduction.

Relevant tickets / context:
- RINF-2345: telemetry histogram schema change (adds microbatch_id).
- RINF-2412: investigate tail spikes after CUDA-graph rollout.

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Consider adding a "slice reporter" endpoint in the runtime that emits top-3 kernel causes for the slowest 1% of requests per minute. Could feed into Optimize for automatic recommendations.
- Keep snapshotting a few Nsight captures per release candidate of graph-enabled runtime; they are small (3s) but high-signal.

If anyone wants raw exports or the slice scripts, ping me (Aisha) or check the linked GitHub PR.

-- Aisha
